prize_parts.citation: for empirical analyses of how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: The work gives a measurable, causally identified account of who gains and who loses when technology and trade change an economy. It joins the task-based view of labour demand to the China-shock evidence on local labour markets, which showed that adjustment costs can be large and persistent in specific regions. The designs are transparent, have been replicated and criticised for more than a decade, and have been emulated widely. The question is first-order for economic policy: how societies handle workers displaced by structural change. In the opening round this ballot had the broadest support across members of different fields. Ten of eleven members ranked it, and seven placed it in their top three. I treat that only as a sign that the case holds up under varied scrutiny, not as evidence of merit. The attribution for the China-shock strand is also clean. Autor, Dorn and Hanson are the joint authors of the central papers, so a three-person citation names those who produced the discovery.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the central quantitative claims are still contested. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, the sensitivity of shift-share designs, and the long-run interpretation of local adjustment are all debated. Credit for the task framework is also shared with scholars outside the credited set, notably Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu was recognised in 2024. The Committee could reasonably judge that the technology-and-labour theme sits close to recent prizes (2021, 2023 and 2024), and that a prize here would be an empirical-design prize rather than a conceptual one. If the task framework and the trade-shock evidence are weighed separately, the citation could end up overstated.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B022 first but would limit the award to Autor and Hanson. He regards Autor as central to both strands, sees Hanson as the core of the China-shock work, and treats Dorn as a more junior co-author.
responses.response: I agree Autor is the common thread and Hanson is the trade-side anchor. But Dorn is a full co-author of the central China-shock papers, so omitting him would leave an attribution gap in the strand that is best documented and most replicated. Seniority is not the criterion. The question is who produced the discovery. A narrower, Autor-and-Hanson citation is defensible if the Committee anchors the prize on the task-and-trade synthesis, and I would not oppose it. I think the three-person version is more faithful to the evidence, and the profile gives me no reason to think the Committee would be constrained by it.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B022 third and proposes Autor, Hanson and Katz. His reasoning is that Katz is central to the skill-premium and technology-race literature, and that Dorn is a defensible alternative.
responses.response: Katz's contribution to the skill premium and to education against technology is real and foundational. I think it is a different discovery from the China-shock evidence, and its credit overlaps with earlier recognised work on education and technology. He also appears on B014 through the Moving to Opportunity work, so his claims could be handled there instead. Adding Katz would move the citation toward a broader labour-demand-and-inequality framing, which widens the attribution dispute rather than resolving it. I would take your swap seriously only if the Committee decides the prize should rest on the long-run skill-biased-change literature rather than the trade-shock evidence.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B014 first and B022 second. She values new population-scale data combined with credible quasi-experimental design on a big question, and she treats the mobility programme as mature enough despite its recency.
responses.response: I share your criterion. I ranked B014 fourth because it resembles work I admire, where new data is built and modern causal methods are applied. My difference with you is maturity. Most of the core mobility results are about a decade old, and the causal reading of neighbourhood effects is still being tested. Credit within a large team is also harder to divide, since I had to leave Friedman and Katz out of my own pair. B022 has had longer to be replicated and criticised, and its attribution to named co-authors is clearer. I would keep B014 as a serious alternative, and it could become the stronger case in a few years.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B029 first. He argues that structural demand estimation and dynamic industry models made empirical industrial organisation quantitative and are standard tools in merger review and antitrust, with the BLP trio as the cleanest attribution.
responses.response: The practical reach of the BLP framework is clear and the attribution to Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes is cleaner than most. I did not rank B029 in my opening because my own assessment weighed the substantive discovery and its consequences for understanding economic change above a methods contribution. I accept that this is a judgement about criteria and not a flaw in your case. The seven-name ballot also leaves Bresnahan, Benkard, Reiss and Levin outside any three-person cap. I would like to hear how you separate the methods contribution from the empirical findings it enabled, and I would reconsider B029 if that argument is strong.

uncertainties: How far the persistence and magnitude of the China-shock effects hold up in re-analyses and in other countries and periods.
Whether the Committee wants the citation anchored on the task framework, the trade-shock evidence, or both, and how the credit then divides among Autor, Hanson, Dorn and Katz.
Whether thematic proximity to the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes on labour-market methods, gender and technology and institutions reduces the marginal case.
Whether the task-framework credit owed to scholars outside the credited set, such as Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane, undermines a clean citation.
I have not independently verified the details of the contributions or the replication record. My assessments rest on the supplied evidence and general background knowledge.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in economic history, covering regional growth, railways, electrification and labour conflict, and nothing in the profile links me to Autor, Hanson or Dorn, or to the alternatives named. I also note that Tommy Andersson is a Lund colleague, but the profile shows no connection between him and any shortlisted candidate or between us on this ballot.
